newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada separatist party struggles with unity.
newsitem.headline: Canada separatist party struggles with unity.

text.p: The Bloc Quebecois, a Quebec separatist party that forms the official opposition in Canada's parliament, ended its convention on Sunday with a new leader and questions about party unity.
Gilles Duceppe, a 49-year-old former communist and son of a popular Quebec actor, won the leadership on Saturday with 53 percent of the votes mailed in by 50,000 of the party's 113,000 members.
By Sunday he was fending off questions about unity in the party which advocates the separation of the French-speaking province of Quebec.

One Bloc member of parliament, Nic LeBlanc, said he would resign the party and sit as an independent, mainly because as a businessman he was not comfortable with Duceppe's active membership in the Communist Workers' Party during the 1970s and 1980s.

LeBlanc's resignation would leave the Bloc tied with the Western Canada-based Reform Party with 50 seats each in the House of Commons. One more Bloc resignation would allow Reform to claim official opposition status heading into what is widely expected to be a June federal election.

In the most dramatic moment of the three-day convention, Yves Duhaime, who finished second to Duceppe for the leadership with 34 percent of the votes, publicly refused to rally to his new leader's side. Even when pressed by reporters, Duhaime refused to endorse Duceppe.
"Party unity must not be something that is a dream. It must be linked to reality and you must deserve it," Duhaime said.

At a news conference on Sunday Duceppe dismissed suggestions that the Bloc membership is divided on a number of important issues, including its leadership and strategy on advancing Quebec independence.
"For me, there is unity in the caucus. It's very clear. You will see the result the Bloc will get (in the election) and it's spirit," Duceppe said.

Duceppe said he will meet with Duhaime in the coming days to discuss his role in the party. Duhaime, who is not an MP, previously said he would run as Bloc candidate in the Saint-Maurice, Quebec, electoral district long held by Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien.

Quebec separatists lost a referendum on Quebec separation in October 1995 by one percentage point. The Parti Quebecois government in Quebec has said it plans to hold another referendum on independence after the next Quebec provincial election, which may be held next year.
